result: Prior work has established that genetic defects in cytoskeletal components cause morphological distortions in C. elegans neurons. Specifically, UNC-70 β-spectrin mutations cause axon fracture in motor neurons and buckling in TRNs, while mutations in mec-17 α-tubulin acetyltransferase and mec-12 α-tubulin cause bends and kinks in TRNs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are all supported by citations to prior published work (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Krieg et al., 2014; Topalidou et al., 2012; Hsu et al., 2014). These claims establish the background context for the current study and are appropriately attributed to previous research.

result: Mutants lacking MT bundles in TRNs do not show shape distortions, suggesting that defects in MT bundles, rather than their absence, cause shape distortions.
evaluation: Claim C5 is supported by citations to prior work and data from Figure 1A. Claim C6 is a logical inference from C5 that is well-supported by the observation that shape distortions occur only when MT bundles are defective, not when they are absent entirely.

result: The study characterizes two key alleles: unc-70(e524) encodes a missense mutation (E2008K) in β-spectrin, and mec-7(wy116) encodes a T409I substitution in β-tubulin that maps to the α-β tubulin interface region.
evaluation: Claim C7 is supported by citation to prior work (Krieg et al., 2014). Claims C8 and C9 are supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2. The molecular characterization of these alleles is well-documented.

result: Single mutants of mec-7(wy116) and ptl-1(ok621) have straight TRNs, but double mutants with unc-70(e524) display large bends, kinks, helices, loops, and plectonemes. These defects are largely absent in mec-12(e1607);unc-70(e524) double mutants that lack 15pf MTs.
evaluation: Claims C12-C16 are supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B, and Video 1. The observation that shape defects require both spectrin and microtubule defects is a key finding. The control experiment with mec-12(e1607) (C14) strengthens the conclusion that intact but defective MT bundles are required for the phenotype.

result: Shape defects in ptl-1;unc-70 double mutants appear at regular intervals (~13 μm), are dynamic, and reorganize following laser axotomy, with evidence of rotation indicative of release from a twisted state.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by quantitative measurements and data shown in Figure 1 and Videos 5-6. The regular spacing, dynamic nature, and response to axotomy provide strong evidence for a mechanical model involving torque and tension.

result: In wild-type animals, AVM axons are positioned far from the neutral bending axis (z = 21.1 ± 6.5 μm) while ALM axons are closer (z = 5.5 ± 1.7 μm). Based on Euler beam theory, AVM axons are predicted to experience four-fold greater deformation than ALM axons, which is confirmed by observations showing AVM undergoes up to 50% strain during locomotion while ALM shows only modest strain changes.
evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2A. Claim C24 is a theoretical prediction based on established beam bending theory. Claims C25-C26 are supported by data in Figure 2B-C and Videos 7-8, confirming the theoretical prediction. The integration of theory and experiment is well-executed.

result: In him-4 mutants, ALM is displaced to the dorsal midline (z = 17 ± 2.6 μm), and both AVM and ALM generate similar local contractions and extensions during locomotion, suggesting that AVM and ALM have similar mechanical properties and that axon position dramatically affects bending-induced mechanical stress.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by data in Figure 2D-F and Videos 9-10. Claims C29-C30 are well-supported inferences from the observation that repositioning ALM causes it to behave mechanically like AVM. This is a clever genetic experiment that tests the positional hypothesis.

result: In unc-70 mutants, AVM axons undergo buckling under compressive stress but ALM axons do not, likely because ALM is positioned near the neutral bending axis. In him-4;unc-70 double mutants where ALM is repositioned, both AVM and ALM exhibit buckling, supporting the idea that mechanical stress depends on anatomical position.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by prior work (Krieg et al., 2014) and data in Figure 3A-C and Videos 11-12. Claim C34 is a reasonable inference. Claim C35 is supported by data in Figure 3E-F and Videos 13-14. Claim C36 is a well-supported conclusion from the combined observations. The experimental design effectively tests the positional hypothesis.

result: AFM measurements show that ptl-1(ok621) and mec-7(wy116) mutant axons have significantly lower Young's moduli (4.6 ± 0.6 kPa and 4.3 ± 0.4 kPa, respectively) compared to wild-type (6.1 ± 0.3 kPa), demonstrating that axonal stiffness depends on both the actin-spectrin cytoskeleton and MT bundles.
evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by quantitative AFM measurements reported in the text. Claim C41 is a well-supported inference from these measurements combined with prior observations on spectrin mutants. The sample sizes (n=11-18) appear adequate for these measurements.

result: Discrete elastic rod (DER) simulations predict that axons will appear straight when twisted if they have sufficient bending stiffness and axial tension, but reducing either parameter leads to localized helices at low twist and plectonemes at high twist. Simulated axons display multiple plectonemes at ~10-20 μm intervals, similar to experimental observations.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by numerical simulations shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures. The simulations are based on established Euler-Kirchhoff theory and the DER model. The agreement between simulated and observed plectoneme spacing (C42) provides validation of the model. However, the model relies on estimated parameters that may have substantial uncertainty.

result: STED microscopy reveals that α- and β-spectrin form periodic structures in wild-type C. elegans TRNs with spacing of 197 ± 13 nm and 199 ± 10 nm, respectively, suggesting the spectrin tetramer is at its fully extended contour length.
evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by quantitative STED measurements shown in Figure 5 and Video 16, with appropriate statistical testing (p=0.64, Mann-Whitney test). Claim C46 is a reasonable inference from the measured spacing. The measurements are consistent with prior work in mammalian neurons.

result: Periodic spectrin structures are eliminated by Latrunculin A treatment or loss of UNC-70 β-spectrin. In unc-70(e524) mutants, α-spectrin maintains periodicity but with a shorter period (188 ± 13 nm), consistent with decreased axial tension. Loss of ptl-1 has no effect on spectrin distribution, indicating spectrin forms a periodic structure sensitive to axial tension but not microtubule defects.
evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by data in Figure 5C-F. Claim C50 is a well-supported inference linking the shorter period to prior measurements of reduced tension. Claim C51 is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2. Claim C52 is a well-supported conclusion from the combined observations. The statistical testing is appropriate (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.003).

result: In wild-type TRNs, microtubules are organized in a hexagonal bundle with edge-to-edge spacing following a log-normal distribution (geometric mean 9.8 nm). In mec-7(wy116) mutants, the geometric mean decreases to 4 nm with nearly three-fold increased variance, and individual MTs often separate from the bundle and contact one another, though hexagonal organization is maintained.
evaluation: Claims C53-C58 are supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 6A-B. The statistical analysis of inter-MT angles using Watson U2 test is appropriate for circular data. The observation that hexagonal organization persists despite altered spacing and MT-MT contacts is interesting and well-documented.

result: In ptl-1(ok621) mutants, MTs are closer together (geometric mean 6.7 nm, variance 81 nm²) and adjacent MTs often collapse onto one another, though hexagonal geometry is largely maintained. Both mec-7 and ptl-1 mutants have fewer and shorter microtubules than wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by EM data in Figure 6D. Claim C63 is supported by data in Figure 6F-G and supplementary figures. The quantitative analysis of MT organization is thorough and well-documented. Sample sizes (13-25 sections from at least 5 datasets per genotype) appear adequate.

result: Based on theoretical considerations that bundle stiffness is proportional to filament number, the observed reduction in MT number and length in mec-7 and ptl-1 mutants suggests decreased bending stiffness. The observation that MTs contact one another in mutants suggests loss of a spacer molecule, which would reduce cross-sectional area and further decrease bending stiffness.
evaluation: Claims C64 and C67 are supported by citations to theoretical work (Bathe et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2007; Tolomeo and Holley, 1997). Claims C65, C66, and C68 are reasonable inferences from the structural observations. However, these are theoretical predictions that would benefit from direct experimental validation through additional mechanical measurements.

result: In ptl-1 and ptl-1;unc-70 mutants, outer MTs rotate and tilt away from the central axis, generating a twist of the entire MT bundle. The pitch angle increases linearly with radius from the bundle center, and helical perversions (reversals between clockwise and counter-clockwise twists) are observed. These findings indicate ptl-1 mutant axons have both decreased bending stiffness and increased torque.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by EM data and PIV analysis shown in Figure 7D and Video 17. The quantitative analysis of helical pitch is innovative and well-executed. Claims C72-C73 are well-supported inferences from the structural observations combined with the mechanical measurements and simulations.

result: FRAP experiments show PTL-1 has an apparent diffusion constant of 0.12 ± 0.1 μm²/s in wild-type axons. Both recovery rate and mobile fraction increase in mec-7(ok2152) and mec-7(wy116) mutants but are unaffected in unc-70(e524) mutants. This supports the idea that PTL-1 binds to MTs in vivo and that the T409I mutation in MEC-7 β-tubulin interferes with PTL-1 binding.
evaluation: Claim C74 is supported by FRAP measurements with adequate sample size (n=47) and agreement with prior work. Claims C75-C76 are supported by data in Figure 8. Claim C77 is a reasonable inference from the differential effects of mec-7 vs. unc-70 mutations. Claims C78-C79 are well-supported inferences from the FRAP data. The logic that wy116 affects PTL-1 affinity rather than just MT number is sound.

result: MTs are shorter in AVM neurons than ALM neurons in wild-type animals, suggesting mechanical stress may limit MT length. In unc-70 mutants, neither the e524 nor s1502 allele causes further reduction in AVM MT length or number, but both are associated with decreased MT length in ALM neurons.
evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by EM data in Figure 9D, Table 2, and supplementary figures. Claim C81 is a reasonable inference linking the shorter AVM MTs to the greater mechanical stress experienced by AVM. Claims C82-C83 are supported by data in Figure 9D-E. The differential effects on AVM vs. ALM are consistent with the positional stress hypothesis.

result: The variance in MT number is higher in unc-70(s1502) mutant ALM neurons than in wild-type or unc-70(e524), which is interpreted as indicating that some long MTs persist because mechanical stresses are decreased while others are shortened due to loss of actin-spectrin networks.
evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by statistical analysis (F-test, p=0.01 and p=0.05) and data in Figure 9F. Claim C85 is a speculative interpretation that attempts to reconcile the increased variance with the different mechanical properties of e524 vs. s1502 mutants. While plausible, this interpretation would benefit from additional supporting evidence.

result: Epidermal expression of wild-type UNC-70 does not rescue MT length in unc-70(e524) mutants but appears to restore MT length in unc-70(s1502) mutants. This suggests the e524 mutant β-spectrin acts dominantly to interfere with mechanical stabilization, and that longer ALM MTs are more susceptible to bending-induced fracture than shorter AVM MTs. The actin-spectrin network provides lateral support protecting MT bundles via both cell-autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by data in Table 2 and Figure 9D-E. Claim C88 is a speculative explanation for the differential rescue that is plausible but not directly tested. Claims C89-C90 are reasonable inferences from the combined observations. The non-autonomous rescue in s1502 but not e524 is an interesting observation that supports a dominant-negative model for e524.

result: Shape defects in ptl-1;unc-70 double mutants are more pronounced at 20°C than 15°C. In ptl-1;unc-70;mec-7(e1434) triple mutants, axons are smooth at the restrictive temperature (20°C) where MT assembly is defective, indicating that formation of loops, twists, and plectonemes depends on intact microtubules.
evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by data in Figure 10A-B. Claim C93 is a well-supported inference from the temperature-sensitive experiment. This is a clever genetic test showing that the shape defects require intact MTs, supporting the model that torque arises from twisted MT bundles.

result: The study concludes that actin-spectrin networks provide tension, MT bundles confer stiffness, and microtubule-associated proteins like tau minimize torque within MT bundles, and these factors combine to protect axons from mechanical damage.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing the experimental and theoretical results. These conclusions are well-supported by the combined evidence from genetics, microscopy, mechanical measurements, and simulations. The integration of multiple approaches provides strong support for this mechanistic model.

result: Simulations based on Euler-Kirchhoff theory show that the balance of tension and torque stabilizes axons and dendrites, and that plectonemes result when torque overcomes tension.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by numerical simulations shown in Figure 4A. The simulations are based on established physical theory and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding the experimental observations. The agreement between simulation and experiment strengthens the conclusions.

result: UNC-70 β-spectrin forms an extended cytoskeleton similar to mammalian neurons and is essential for maintaining proper axial tension.
evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by data from this study and citations to prior work (D'Este et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2013). Claim C101 is supported by citation to prior work (Krieg et al., 2014). These claims establish the conserved role of spectrin in neuronal mechanics.

result: PTL-1 tau has a MT-binding domain and an intrinsically disordered N-terminal projection domain with glutamate/proline repeats proposed to function as a polyelectrolyte brush. The data suggest PTL-1 enables MTs to glide past one another during mechanical stress by preventing MT-MT contact and thus friction and torque generation.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by citation to prior work (Chung et al., 2015). Claim C103 is supported by citation to prior work (Wegmann et al., 2013). Claims C104-C105 are well-supported inferences from the structural observations of MT bundles in ptl-1 mutants. The model that PTL-1 prevents MT-MT contact to allow sliding is consistent with all observations.

result: The twisted MT bundle structures in ptl-1 mutants are similar to bundles predicted to assemble from chiral biological polymers. The authors propose that torque is an emergent property of MT assembly that appears in the absence of PTL-1, with MTs twisting to maximize cohesive energy. This mechanism is expected to be independent of protofilament number.
evaluation: Claim C106 is a reasonable inference supported by citation to theoretical work (Grason and Bruinsma, 2007). Claims C107-C109 are speculative proposals about the mechanism of torque generation. While plausible and consistent with the observations, these mechanistic claims lack direct experimental validation. The proposal that torque is an emergent property of MT assembly would benefit from additional testing.

result: MT bundles and actin-spectrin networks act synergistically to prevent shape defects, as deficiency in both structures is required for plectoneme appearance.
evaluation: Claim C110 is a well-supported inference from the observation that plectonemes appear only in double mutants affecting both the actin-spectrin network and MT bundles. This synergistic relationship is a key finding of the study.

result: The authors propose that the mechanisms protecting C. elegans neurons may also protect mammalian neurons from mechanical stress during daily life or traumatic brain injury. They note that spectrin, microtubules, and tau are conserved and abundant in all animal nervous systems, and that mechanical stress and defects in these proteins have been implicated in neurodegenerative disease.
evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by citations (Baines, 2009; Findeisen et al., 2014). Claims C113-C114 are supported by citations to prior work. Claims C112 and C115 are speculative extrapolations from C. elegans to mammalian systems and human disease. While the conservation of these proteins supports the possibility of conserved mechanisms, direct evidence in mammalian systems is lacking. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not demonstrated by the current study.
